assessment_summary:
Step 1: Let T be an arbitrary tournament on exactly 4 vertices.
Justification 1: Justified. (Sets up the premise).
Step 2: A tournament is a directed graph where every pair of distinct vertices is joined by exactly one arc.
Justification 2: Justified. (Definition of a tournament).
Step 3: By Rédei's Theorem, every tournament has at least one directed Hamiltonian path.
Justification 3: Justified. (Application of a standard graph theory theorem).
Step 4: Let this Hamiltonian path in T be denoted as v_1 -> v_2 -> v_3 -> v_4.
Justification 4: Justified. (Naming the path guaranteed by Step 3).
Step 5: Because T is a tournament, there must be exactly one directed arc between v_1 and v_4.
Justification 5: Justified. (By definition of a tournament).
Step 6: In a tournament, the arc connecting the start and end of a Hamiltonian path is always directed from the end to the start.
Justification 6: Objection. False. In a transitive tournament, the arc between the path's start and end is directed from start to end.
Step 7: Therefore, the arc between v_1 and v_4 is directed as v_4 -> v_1.
Justification 7: Objection. Relies on the false claim in Step 6.
Step 8: Adding the arc v_4 -> v_1 to the Hamiltonian path yields the directed cycle v_1 -> v_2 -> v_3 -> v_4 -> v_1.
Justification 8: Justified. (If the arc existed, it would correctly form this cycle).
Step 9: This cycle visits all 4 vertices exactly once, so it is a Hamiltonian cycle.
Justification 9: Justified. (Matches the definition of a Hamiltonian cycle).
Step 10: Since T was arbitrary, every tournament on 4 vertices contains a Hamiltonian cycle.
Justification 10: Objection. The conclusion relies on Step 6, which is invalid.
counterexample: The transitive tournament on 4 vertices (where vertices are 1, 2, 3, 4 and arcs are i -> j for all 1 <= i < j <= 4) has no Hamiltonian cycle, as vertex 4 has out-degree 0 and therefore cannot be part of any directed cycle.
